new_statements.quote: Stress is on the first syllable of two and three-syllable words with some exceptions. When the primary stress occurs on the first syllable of three-syllable words, there will be a secondary stress on the third syllable. Two and three-syllable names also have stress on the first syllable with some exceptions. [...] Phonemically I will write stress only on words that are exceptions to this generalization. [p.42] In four-syllable words, the primary stress will occur on the third syllable with a secondary stress on the first syllable. The exceptions have primary stress on the second syllable and secondary stress on the fourth syllable. Compounds may or may not retain their original stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress is word-initial: 2- and 3-syllable words (including names) are stressed on the first syllable, 3-syllable words adding a secondary stress on the third; 4-syllable words carry primary stress on the third syllable with secondary on the first (i.e. alternating from the left edge, with the rightmost beat promoted in 4-syllable words). A lexically listed minority of words deviate (2nd-syllable stress in disyllables such as ka'sek 'little', ku'pik 'skin', kam'bom 'bad', ba'lam 'sweet potato'; 2nd+4th in some 4-syllable words), and Muzzey marks stress in phonemic transcription only on these exceptions. The later OPD (Muzzey 1992, rev. Lindstrom 2008) restates this more cautiously: stress is 'often on the first syllable of two and three-syllable words, but it is not fully predictable.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: 3-syllable words: secondary stress on the 3rd syllable when primary is on the 1st; 4-syllable words: primary on 3rd, secondary on 1st (exceptional pattern: primary 2nd, secondary 4th); 4-syllable compounds may have secondary stress on the 4th syllable (1979: 'kubahen'vi 'Friday'); compounds may or may not retain the stress of their members.
new_statements.exceptions: Listed exceptions with non-initial stress: ka.'sek 'little', ku.'pik 'skin', kam.'bom 'bad', ke.'den 'quickly', ka.'ka.pin 'insect', La.'pun (name), xa.'ian.da 'he scolds', xa.'iu.mik 'he whistled'; 4-syllable exceptions ia.'xa.bu.'tin 'I tie', Ya.'nak.da.'bin (name); OPD adds [bɑˈlɑm] 'sweet potato', [ioˈβɑ] 'smoke', [guɑsiˈlim] 'trap'. Stress shifts onto the syllable where a vowel is deleted under suffixation/contraction (p.43: 'ia.xa + eik -> ia.'xeik 'I sleep'). 1979: 'Occasionally stress will shift from the normal pattern, and more study is needed' (du'viyaŋ 'earthquake').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on isolated (citation) forms; Muzzey 1979 uses the stress pattern explicitly as a criterion for word boundaries. Syllable-count-dependent placement (initial in 2-3 syllable words, third syllable in 4-syllable words). No tone or contrastive length reported (OPD 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' mentions only stress); unstressed syllables may be phonetically compressed ('Timing', p.42).
new_statements.identity_note: Muzzey's 1979 and 1988 descriptions are based on fieldwork in Yemli village, i.e. the Hote dialect proper (Glottolog 'Nuclear Hote' nucl1515), not the Misim dialect (misi1244); she treats Hote, Yamap and Misim as three dialects of one language. The OPD header calls the language 'Malê [HOT]' (Ethnologue name Malei), population figure 'includes 1,909 Hote and 328 Misim'.

sources.note: Sec. 1.1 'Stress patterns' (p.7, used as a word-boundary criterion): 'In words of one to four syllables, primary stress usually occurs on the first syllable' ('damak 'lightning', 'dumloli 'mountain'); four-syllable words rarely occur but have secondary stress on the third syllable ('kate'poli 'potato'); four-syllable compounds may have secondary stress on the fourth ('kubahen'vi 'Friday'); 'Occasionally stress will shift from the normal pattern, and more study is needed to determine the reason for this' (du'viyaŋ 'earthquake').
